old: One 19th-century scientist needed a name for a plan rendered in a single, unmistakable hue.
It joins a color and a mark left by pressing something onto paper.
Its two halves are simply 'blue' and 'print,' fused by Sir John Herschel in 1842.
clues: This noun for a kind of plan was introduced by an astronomer, Sir John Herschel, a surprising origin for a word now tied to builders and engineers.
More exact than a rough sketch or outline, it is the detailed technical drawing architects and engineers work from, or any thorough guide to achieving something.
Its name recalls the color these copies once literally came out, and today people speak of a detailed one for success, for peace, or for life itself.
